go over and over why the event happened to me
I dwell on how I used to be before the event

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.
When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.

vignette: Eleanor Vance spent forty-two years commanding freighters across the North Atlantic, but it was a Tuesday afternoon in Boston Harbor that unraveled her life. She had been reviewing manifest papers at a waterfront consulate when two municipal officers approached her over a routine zoning complaint. What began as a verbal exchange curdled when one officer misread her directive hand signals as a physical threat. In seconds, she was pinned against the damp brick wall of the loading dock, the weight of a baton across her shoulders, the sharp crack of a flashlight beam in her eyes, and the unyielding command to remain prone despite her decades of maritime authority. The incident was eventually dismissed as a procedural error, but for Eleanor, the loss of control had been absolute, and the harbor that once felt like an extension of her ship now felt like a grid of potential threats. In the months that followed, the dock environment became impossible to navigate without her mind fracturing. Every time she walked the gangplanks of the retired vessel she kept moored at Pier 4, the sound of heavy boots striking wet concrete would instantly pull her backward. Her memories of the frightening event were very clear and detailed, arriving not as hazy recollections but as a series of sharp, photographic recall images locked in her mind. She could still see the exact scuff on the officer’s boot, the way the flashlight reflected off the seawater, the unblinking glare in his eyes. These vivid, detailed images arrived unbidden, and when they did, the present dissolved entirely. Eleanor felt the cold brick at her back, heard the authoritative commands in her ears, and braced for the blow, as if the event were happening right now rather than decades ago. Because these intrusive, hyper-detailed memories would surface without warning, Eleanor found herself unable to tolerate quiet. The relentless clarity of those mental snapshots forced her to throw herself into work, drilling bolts and polishing brass until her fingers ached, then moving to the local maritime archive to catalog shipping logs and keep her mind occupied. With that frantic activity as a buffer, she would eventually sit alone, automatically going over and over why the event happened to her, dissecting the officers’ commands, the weather conditions, and her own posture until the relentless analysis became her only coping mechanism. Yet the very habits she adopted to quiet her mind only ensured the memories remained active. Every hour she spent overworking at the docks and every evening consumed by rumination acted as continuous rehearsal, which in turn fed directly back into her memory system, sharpening the photographic recall and making the reliving episodes more frequent. When she returned to the pier to inspect cargo cranes at the maritime institute where she volunteered, the mental preparation she had built through days of frantic work would immediately cue the old footage, and she would feel the event unfolding right now, her body bracing against the wall exactly as it had decades ago. Her avoidance had become a self-sustaining current. Over the years, this cycle carved a quiet but profound gulf between Eleanor and the life she had known. She found herself constantly dwelling on how she used to be before the event, watching the vibrant woman who once navigated by the stars and laughed with fellow captains at the wharf tavern vanish behind a wall of frantic tasks and mental rehearsals. Her late husband’s memory, which she had once tended with fond routine, now felt overshadowed by a grief she could not articulate through analysis. At seventy-six, Eleanor finally walked into the clinical practice after a particularly severe episode during a routine supply run to her boat. As a delivery driver’s shouted instructions echoed across the pier, she had dropped her crate and spent the next twenty minutes gripping the gunwale, certain she was back on the loading dock. She sought help not because she wanted to relive the past, but because she was terrified of becoming entirely disconnected from her own life. What she hoped for was a way to look at the harbor without seeing the flashlights, to navigate her days without drowning in the relentless, photographic past, and to finally rest without bracing for a threat that had long since moved on.
